title: It's a jug
hook: if you love a jug, say "I love a jug," and if it breaks you won't be thrown (Enchiridion 3)
carry: clay breaks; that's part of what clay is

segments.voice: Yesterday: desire, held lightly. Your line was gently, for now. Did you add the quiet clause to a plan: if nothing prevents me? Day three hundred thirty-five.

A mug that nobody else is allowed to use. Chipped, maybe. A gift, maybe. Somebody's grandmother's. One morning it slips off the counter, and the small crack on the tile floor can land like bad news. It's a mug. Everyone in the kitchen knows it's a mug. And still. Epictetus, teaching in a Greek town, picked almost exactly this object to start with. Not a great loss. A clay pot from the kitchen. Today: it's a jug.
screen: `THE MUG NOBODY ELSE USES.` → `A CRACK ON THE TILE.` → `IT'S A JUG.`

segments.voice: First, the instruction. In section three of the handbook, Epictetus says: with everything that delights you, or is useful, or that you love, remind yourself what kind of thing it is. And start with the smallest things. If you're fond of a jug, say: I'm fond of a jug. Then when it breaks, you won't be thrown. Second, the point isn't to love it less. You can still drink from the good mug every morning. The practice is to name it truly while you have it. Clay breaks; that's part of what clay is. When you've said so ahead of time, the breaking is a sad thing that happened, not a betrayal. Third, the hard part. The same section doesn't stop at jugs. Epictetus goes on: when you kiss your child or your wife, say to yourself that you are kissing a human being, and then if one of them dies, you won't be overwhelmed. Readers argue about this line. Some find it cold, a way of guarding the heart against the people it should be open to. Others hear it as tender: everyone you love is mortal, and saying so can make each goodbye at the door count. The text itself doesn't settle it, and you don't have to either. Fourth, why he starts small. Epictetus is a trainer. Nobody lifts the heaviest weight on the first day. Practice on the jug, the phone screen, the favorite sweater. Learn the move where it costs little. That's why the handbook says: begin with the smallest things.
screen: `SAY WHAT KIND OF THING IT IS.` · `LOVE IT, AND NAME IT TRULY.` · `THE HARD LINE: A HUMAN BEING.` · `BEGIN WITH THE SMALLEST THINGS.` · then, large: `IT'S A JUG.`

segments.voice: Look around you and choose one small thing you're fond of. A cup, a pen, a pair of shoes, a plant. If you can, hold it, or rest your eyes on it. Now name it plainly, the way Epictetus would. This is a cup, and cups break. Say it without coldness, the way you'd say it's raining. Then notice what's left: you still like it. Maybe you like it a little more. Stay with the thing and the breath. The bell holds the time.
Epictetus, whose small practice names what you love for what it is, starting with the smallest things, so its breaking doesn't throw you. Today's word.
Your line: clay breaks; that's part of what clay is. When something small breaks, spills or goes missing today, say the line once before anything else. Day three hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism name a cherished object plainly to themselves, 'this is a cup, and cups break', practicing on small things first.

original.note: Greek, Enchiridion 3: an earthenware pot or jug.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't get attached to stuff.
what it means: love it, and name what kind of thing it is, starting small, so its breaking doesn't throw you.
what a scholar hears: the same section applies it to a child and a spouse, a line readers still argue over.

notes: Review (2026-10-01): hook no longer tells the listener what they feel and drops the 'nearly two thousand years ago' date; 'argued for centuries' and 'most debated' (unsourced) softened; practice no longer assumes the object is clay.
